questions.t: The devil's advocate was the popular name for the Catholic Church's Promoter of the Faith, an office Pope Sixtus V formally established in 1587 to argue against canonization candidates.
questions.f: The devil's advocate was the popular name for the Catholic Church's Promoter of the Faith, an office Pope John Paul II formally established in 1983 to argue against canonization candidates.
questions.x: Sixtus V created the office in the 16th century; John Paul II's 1983 reform of canonization procedure is when its influence faded. Management researchers later borrowed the idea of an assigned critic for strategic planning.

questions.t: A 1986 laboratory study found devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry groups made better strategic recommendations than consensus groups, but consensus groups were more satisfied.
questions.f: A 1986 laboratory study found consensus groups made better strategic recommendations than devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry groups, but were less satisfied.
questions.x: Structured conflict raised decision quality and scrutiny of assumptions at a social cost: consensus groups reported more satisfaction and more acceptance of the final decision. Managers using the method have to manage that trade-off.

questions.t: Nemeth, Rogers and Brown reported in 2001 that no role-played dissent generates as much divergent thinking as authentic dissent.
questions.f: Nemeth, Rogers and Brown reported in 2001 that role-played devil's advocacy generates more divergent thinking than authentic dissent.
questions.x: Assigned critics are seen as playing a part, so their objections carry less weight than a colleague's real disagreement. That is why assigning a critic should complement, not replace, a climate where people voice their own concerns.

questions.t: In the bargain-then-ripoff pattern, firms price low, even below cost, to win unattached buyers, then charge more once those buyers are locked in.
questions.f: In the bargain-then-ripoff pattern, firms price high to win unattached buyers, then cut prices once those buyers are locked in to keep them from leaving.
questions.x: A locked-in customer tolerates a higher price before leaving, so early share becomes later profit. In the simplest model, competition for new customers passes those later rents back through the early discounts.

questions.t: Farrell and Klemperer treat contractual switching costs, such as frequent-flyer programs, as created by firms rather than as real social costs.
questions.f: Farrell and Klemperer treat learning switching costs, such as mastering new software, as created by firms rather than as real social costs.
questions.x: A loyalty rebate is a transfer a firm engineers to discourage switching; society would lose nothing if it vanished. Learning costs, by contrast, are real resources spent and are paid once.

questions.t: The EU Data Act lets cloud providers recover switching and data-egress costs only during a transition ending on 12 January 2027, after which such charges must go.
questions.f: The EU Data Act lets cloud providers recover switching and data-egress costs indefinitely, provided the charges do not exceed the provider's actual cost.
questions.x: Regulators cut switching costs when lock-in limits competition. The Act, applying since September 2025, phases out egress fees entirely, much as U.S. number portability did for mobile subscribers.

questions.t: Barbara Minto developed the Pyramid Principle while editing consultants' reports at McKinsey in London, where she kept rearranging their ideas into the same shape.
questions.f: Barbara Minto developed the Pyramid Principle while teaching business writing at Harvard, where she kept rearranging students' essays into the same shape.
questions.x: Minto worked at McKinsey from 1963 to 1973 and turned her editing pattern into an internal course and manual. Her first book on it is dated to 1985, and she later taught it to firms such as Accenture and Bain.

questions.t: One of Minto's three pyramid rules is that an idea at any level must summarize the ideas grouped below it.
questions.f: One of Minto's three pyramid rules is that an idea at any level must introduce a new point not covered by the ideas grouped below it.
questions.x: The other two rules are that grouped ideas must be of the same logical kind and follow a logical order. Summarizing upward is what lets a reader stop at the top and still have the main message.

questions.t: Business communication texts advise an indirect opening, with a buffer before the news, when a message will strongly affect the reader or the writer does not know them well.
questions.f: Business communication texts advise an indirect opening, with a buffer before the news, when the audience values brevity or already expects the news.
questions.x: Answer-first suits readers who want speed or expect the message. Bad news or an unfamiliar reader can call for explanation first, which is the main limit on applying the pyramid everywhere.

questions.topic: Management by Objectives: Goal-Setting Through Superior-Subordinate Agreement
questions.t: Peter Drucker first set out management by objectives in The Practice of Management in 1954.
questions.f: Peter Drucker first set out management by objectives in The Effective Executive in 1966.
questions.x: In his 1954 book, Drucker argued that effective managers focus on results rather than activity and delegate by agreeing objectives with each subordinate. The idea draws on McGregor's Theory Y view that people can direct their own work.

questions.topic: Management by Objectives: Goal-Setting Through Superior-Subordinate Agreement
questions.t: Rodgers and Hunter found MBO's productivity gains were largest where top management was committed to it and used it themselves, and smallest where leaders paid it lip service.
questions.f: Rodgers and Hunter found MBO's productivity gains were largest where front-line employees designed the program, and smallest where top management drove it themselves.
questions.x: Of 70 cases they reviewed, 68 showed gains, but the size depended on executive commitment. That is why textbooks conclude MBO should be launched from the top down.

questions.topic: Management by Objectives: Goal-Setting Through Superior-Subordinate Agreement
questions.t: In a 1970 HBR article, Harry Levinson argued that MBO wrongly assumes employees' personal aims already match corporate goals, and proposed starting from the employee's own objectives.
questions.f: In a 1970 HBR article, Harry Levinson argued that MBO wrongly assumes corporate goals can be broken into individual targets, and proposed replacing it with team-level quotas.
questions.x: Levinson's critique was psychological: MBO leaves individual needs out of performance measurement and piles pressure on an assumed alignment. He later added that its focus on quantifiable results crowds out qualitative work.

questions.t: In the fourth step of the ASC 606 and IFRS 15 model, the transaction price is allocated to performance obligations in proportion to their stand-alone selling prices.
questions.f: In the fourth step of the ASC 606 and IFRS 15 model, the transaction price is allocated to performance obligations in proportion to their cost to deliver.
questions.x: Allocation by stand-alone selling price splits a bundle as if each good or service had been sold separately. Revenue then arrives only at step five, when each obligation is satisfied.

questions.t: A study of 2016-2019 adoption found that US software firms, not electronic-computer makers, gained comparability and a tighter link between revenue accruals and cash under ASC 606.
questions.f: A study of 2016-2019 adoption found that US electronic-computer makers, not software firms, gained comparability and a tighter link between revenue accruals and cash under ASC 606.
questions.x: Software firms bundle several deliverables across periods, so the new model changed them most; their average adoption adjustment was 4.4% of assets against 1.6% for computer firms. The effects were concentrated rather than universal.

questions.t: When Microsoft adopted the new revenue standard in 2017, Windows 10 revenue once spread over a device's life was instead recognised mainly at billing and delivery.
questions.f: When Microsoft adopted the new revenue standard in 2017, Windows 10 revenue once recognised at billing and delivery was instead spread over a device's life.
questions.x: Microsoft reported a material effect on its income statements and balance sheets but none on cash flows. The lesson is that the timing of reported revenue can shift sharply while cash and underlying economics stay the same.

questions.t: In 1988 the US Department of Labor told Avon's management that the fiduciary duties of ERISA pension plans included proxy voting.
questions.f: In 1988 the US Securities and Exchange Commission told Avon's management that the fiduciary duties of ERISA pension plans included proxy voting.
questions.x: The Labor Department's Avon letter meant pension funds had to vote every ballot item, which created steady demand for outside analysis. ISS, founded in the mid-1980s, was well placed to supply it.

questions.t: Using a cutoff in ISS's own guidelines, Malenko and Shen estimated that a negative ISS say-on-pay recommendation in 2010-2011 cut shareholder support by about 25 percentage points.
questions.f: Using a cutoff in ISS's own guidelines, Malenko and Shen estimated that a negative ISS say-on-pay recommendation in 2010-2011 cut shareholder support by about 2 percentage points.
questions.x: The regression-discontinuity design compares firms just either side of an ISS threshold, isolating the recommendation's causal effect. The large effect is why boards design pay plans with advisor policies in mind.

questions.t: In July 2022 the SEC rescinded the advance-access conditions on proxy advisors' exemptions but kept their conflict-disclosure requirement and anti-fraud liability.
questions.f: In July 2022 the SEC rescinded the conflict-disclosure requirement on proxy advisors' exemptions but kept the advance-access conditions and anti-fraud liability.
questions.x: The 2020 rules had required advisors to disclose conflicts and give companies early access to their advice. The 2022 rollback dropped only the company-access part, showing how US policy has swung back and forth.

questions.t: Thomas Holmes inferred the value of store density from how much sales cannibalization among neighbouring stores Walmart accepted, and found benefits well beyond cheaper trucking.
questions.f: Thomas Holmes inferred the value of store density from how much sales cannibalization among neighbouring stores Walmart accepted, and found benefits limited mainly to cheaper trucking.
questions.x: Walmart kept opening stores close to existing ones even though they took sales from each other, which only makes sense if clustering saves a lot. Holmes concluded those density savings were large and broad, not just shorter delivery routes.

questions.t: From 1982 to 2002, Walmart accounted for almost half the productivity growth in U.S. general merchandise retailing, by Emek Basker's figures.
questions.f: From 1982 to 2002, Walmart accounted for almost a tenth of the productivity growth in U.S. general merchandise retailing, by Emek Basker's figures.
questions.x: Sales per worker rose 54.5 log points at Walmart U.S. versus 18.5 for the rest of the sector. Basker credits technology such as bar-code readers and Retail Link, plus scale.

questions.t: In FY2026 Walmart reported total revenues of $713.2 billion and e-commerce sales of $150.4 billion, up 46%.
questions.f: In FY2026 Walmart reported total revenues of $483.0 billion and e-commerce sales of $150.4 billion, up 46%.
questions.x: $483.0 billion was net sales at Walmart U.S. alone; adding Walmart International and Sam's Club U.S. brings total revenue to $713.2 billion. E-commerce has become a large business inside a store-based company.

questions.t: Applying his risk-adjusted alpha to 115 mutual funds over 1945-1964, Michael Jensen found they did not on average beat buy-and-hold, even before management expenses.
questions.f: Applying his risk-adjusted alpha to 115 mutual funds over 1945-1964, Michael Jensen found they beat buy-and-hold on average, but not after management expenses.
questions.x: Jensen's alpha builds on CAPM to measure return beyond what a portfolio's risk would predict. Finding no edge even before fees was a strong result: managers' forecasting skill added nothing on average.

questions.t: In 1990 Jensen and Kevin Murphy estimated a typical CEO's wealth moved only $3.25 for each $1,000 change in shareholder wealth, and urged more equity pay.
questions.f: In 1990 Jensen and Kevin Murphy estimated a typical CEO's wealth moved about $325 for each $1,000 change in shareholder wealth, and urged less equity pay.
questions.x: They judged such weak sensitivity too small to motivate value creation. Murphy later recalled that firms layered options on top of salary rather than swapping one for the other, which drove CEO pay sharply higher.

questions.t: Jensen argued in 2005 that overvalued equity creates its own agency costs, as managers unable to justify an inflated share price may make value-destroying acquisitions or manage earnings.
questions.f: Jensen argued in 2005 that undervalued equity creates its own agency costs, as managers unable to lift a depressed share price may make value-destroying acquisitions or manage earnings.
questions.x: An inflated price sets expectations the business cannot meet, and big equity stakes make managers reluctant to let it correct. This revised his earlier enthusiasm for heavy equity-based pay.

questions.topic: Business Model: How a Firm Creates, Delivers and Captures Value
questions.t: Casadesus-Masanell and Ricart define strategy as a contingent plan for which business model to use, and the business model as the reflection of the firm's realised strategy.
questions.f: Casadesus-Masanell and Ricart define the business model as a contingent plan for which strategy to use, and strategy as the reflection of the firm's realised business model.
questions.x: In their view every organization has a business model, but not every one has a strategy. Tactics are the residual choices the business model leaves open.

questions.topic: Business Model: How a Firm Creates, Delivers and Captures Value
questions.t: Zott, Amit and Massa's review found that 37% of the business model publications they examined did not define the concept at all.
questions.f: Zott, Amit and Massa's review found that only 7% of the business model publications they examined did not define the concept at all.
questions.x: Only 44% defined it explicitly and 19% borrowed someone else's definition. That inconsistency underlies the critique that the construct is fragmented, which hampers cumulative research.

questions.topic: Business Model: How a Firm Creates, Delivers and Captures Value
questions.t: Hilti moved from selling power tools to leasing managed tool fleets for a monthly fee, which required a new profit formula and much longer sales cycles.
questions.f: Hilti moved from leasing managed tool fleets to selling power tools outright, which required a new profit formula and much shorter sales cycles.
questions.x: The shift illustrates that business model elements are interdependent: changing how value is captured forced changes in resources, processes and how salespeople worked. Sales staff had to be retrained for the new model.

questions.topic: Contracting Officer: Warranted Authority to Bind the Government
questions.t: In Federal Crop Insurance Corp. v. Merrill (1947), the Supreme Court held that anyone dealing with the government bears the risk of confirming an official acts within his authority.
questions.f: In Federal Crop Insurance Corp. v. Merrill (1947), the Supreme Court held that the government bears the risk when its official wrongly assures a private party he acts within his authority.
questions.x: Idaho farmers relied on an agent's wrong assurance that reseeded wheat was covered and were refused payment. Published regulations count as notice to all, a principle the FAR now codifies in its contracting-authority rules.

questions.topic: Contracting Officer: Warranted Authority to Bind the Government
questions.t: A contracting officer's representative handles day-to-day technical oversight but has no power to change a contract's price, quantity, quality or delivery terms.
questions.f: A contracting officer's representative handles day-to-day technical oversight and may change a contract's price, quantity, quality or delivery terms within delegated limits.
questions.x: The COR is delegated monitoring duties in writing, cannot redelegate and can be personally liable for unauthorized acts. Changing contract terms stays with the warranted contracting officer.

questions.topic: Contracting Officer: Warranted Authority to Bind the Government
questions.t: An unauthorized commitment can be ratified only if, among other tests, the government received a benefit and a contracting officer finds the price fair and reasonable.
questions.f: An unauthorized commitment can be ratified only if, among other tests, the official who made it held a warrant and a contracting officer finds the price fair and reasonable.
questions.x: By definition, an unauthorized commitment is made by someone without authority, so a warrant cannot be a condition. Ratification also requires that a proper contract would have been lawful and that funds were available; otherwise the claim goes to claims procedures.

questions.topic: Innovation Management: Organizing the Innovation Process
questions.t: Van de Ven's 1986 Management Science article named managing attention, so that people notice the need for novelty, as the human problem of innovation management.
questions.f: Van de Ven's 1986 Management Science article named managing part-whole relationships, so that people notice the need for novelty, as the human problem of innovation management.
questions.x: He listed four problems: attention (human), turning ideas into accepted practice (process), part-whole relationships as an innovation spreads (structural) and institutional leadership (strategic). The attention problem explains why efficient routines dull sensitivity to new needs.

questions.topic: Innovation Management: Organizing the Innovation Process
questions.t: In Gary Pisano's typology, disruptive innovation needs a new business model but little new technology, while radical innovation needs new technology within the same model.
questions.f: In Gary Pisano's typology, radical innovation needs a new business model but little new technology, while disruptive innovation needs new technology within the same model.
questions.x: Pisano sorts projects on two axes, technology and business model. Routine needs neither and architectural needs both; he argues most firms should hold a deliberate portfolio, since routine innovation can be very profitable.

questions.topic: Innovation Management: Organizing the Innovation Process
questions.t: ISO 56001, published in September 2024, is the first requirements standard for an innovation management system and applies to organizations of any size or sector.
questions.f: ISO 56001, published in September 2024, is the first requirements standard for an innovation management system and applies only to large manufacturers with formal R&D units.
questions.x: The standard treats innovation as an organization-wide system rather than an R&D activity. It uses the same harmonized structure as other ISO management-system standards, so it can sit alongside quality or environmental systems.

questions.topic: Information Asymmetry: Unequal Knowledge Between Transacting Parties
questions.t: Akerlof's 1970 lemons paper showed that when only sellers know a used car's quality, buyers pay for average quality, so owners of good cars withdraw and bad cars drive out good.
questions.f: Akerlof's 1970 lemons paper showed that when only buyers know a used car's quality, sellers price for average quality, so owners of bad cars withdraw and good cars drive out bad.
questions.x: Akerlof called this a modified Gresham's law. With many quality grades the exit of better cars can cascade until no trade happens, even though trade would occur with symmetric information.

questions.topic: Information Asymmetry: Unequal Knowledge Between Transacting Parties
questions.t: An insurer offering lower premiums in exchange for higher deductibles is screening: the uninformed party designs a menu that makes customers reveal their risk.
questions.f: An insurer offering lower premiums in exchange for higher deductibles is signaling: the informed party takes a costly action that reveals its own risk.
questions.x: In screening the uninformed side moves first, and low-risk customers self-select into high deductibles. Signaling runs the other way, as when a worker acquires costly education to show productivity.

questions.topic: Information Asymmetry: Unequal Knowledge Between Transacting Parties
questions.t: Emons and George found privately sold used cars in Basle were more likely than average to have defects while dealer-sold cars were less likely, yet judged the lemons problem not widespread.
questions.f: Emons and George found dealer-sold used cars in Basle were more likely than average to have defects while privately sold cars were less likely, yet judged the lemons problem not widespread.
questions.x: Private sales were about 27% more likely to have defects and dealer sales about 10% less, consistent with dealer reputation acting as a quality guarantee. Few cars were resold at all, so institutions seem to absorb much of the problem.

questions.topic: Brand Equity: The Marketing Value of a Brand Name
questions.t: Customer-based brand equity is the differential effect brand knowledge has on how consumers respond to a brand's marketing, while the financial view measures incremental cash flow.
questions.f: Customer-based brand equity is the incremental cash flow branded products earn over unbranded ones, while the financial view measures consumers' differential response to marketing.
questions.x: Keller's customer-based view looks inside buyers' heads: a brand has positive equity when people react better to its price or advertising than to an unnamed offer. The financial view, used by Simon and Sullivan, isolates the extra cash the brand earns.

questions.topic: Brand Equity: The Marketing Value of a Brand Name
questions.t: In Keller's brand-resonance pyramid, resonance, the loyalty and engagement customers feel, sits at the top above identity, meaning and responses.
questions.f: In Keller's brand-resonance pyramid, identity, who the brand is and what need it meets, sits at the top above meaning, responses and resonance.
questions.x: The pyramid builds from the base: first establish identity, then meaning (performance and imagery), then judgments and feelings, and only then the deep loyalty of resonance.

questions.topic: Brand Equity: The Marketing Value of a Brand Name
questions.t: Ailawadi, Lehmann and Neslin proposed the revenue premium, the extra revenue a brand earns over a comparable private-label product, as a middle-path brand equity measure.
questions.f: Ailawadi, Lehmann and Neslin proposed the price premium, the extra price a brand charges over a comparable private-label product, as a middle-path brand equity measure.
questions.x: Revenue captures both price and volume, so it avoids the subjectivity of mindset surveys and the assumptions of market-value methods. They found it reliable and responsive to real changes in brand strength.

questions.topic: Total Quality Management: Companywide Quality as a Management System
questions.t: The label Total Quality Management was first used by the U.S. Naval Air Systems Command to describe its Japanese-style improvement approach.
questions.f: The label Total Quality Management was first used by Japan's Union of Scientists and Engineers to describe its companywide improvement approach.
questions.x: JUSE invited Deming to lecture in 1950 and created the Deming Prize, but the Japanese term was companywide quality control. The TQM name came later from the U.S. Navy.

questions.topic: Total Quality Management: Companywide Quality as a Management System
questions.t: Powell's 1995 study found TQM's visible tools, like quality training and benchmarking, generally gave no competitive advantage, while open culture, empowerment and executive commitment did.
questions.f: Powell's 1995 study found TQM's visible tools, like quality training and benchmarking, gave competitive advantage, while open culture, empowerment and executive commitment generally did not.
questions.x: Tools are easy to copy, so they cannot set a firm apart; tacit cultural resources are hard to imitate. Powell concluded firms with those resources could outperform with or without the TQM label.

questions.topic: Total Quality Management: Companywide Quality as a Management System
questions.t: Hendricks and Singhal found quality-award winners showed no stock-price edge during implementation but significantly outperformed controls over the following five years.
questions.f: Hendricks and Singhal found quality-award winners outperformed controls during implementation but showed no stock-price edge over the following five years.
questions.x: Mean gains in the later period were roughly 38% to 46% depending on the control group. The lag suggests TQM pays off slowly, which may explain why impatient programs were abandoned.

questions.topic: Goal-Setting Theory: Specific, Difficult Goals and Performance
questions.t: Goal-setting theory began with Edwin Locke's laboratory research in the late 1960s, and Gary Latham carried it into the field, starting with pulpwood logging crews.
questions.f: Goal-setting theory began with Gary Latham's laboratory research in the late 1960s, and Edwin Locke carried it into the field, starting with pulpwood logging crews.
questions.x: Locke's lab studies found specific high goals beat instructions to do one's best; Latham tested the idea with real crews, where productivity and attendance rose within a week. The two consolidated the program into a formal theory in 1990.

questions.topic: Goal-Setting Theory: Specific, Difficult Goals and Performance
questions.t: Latham's field work found that when goal difficulty was held constant, assigned goals performed as well as participatively set ones, especially when a rationale was given.
questions.f: Latham's field work found that even when goal difficulty was held constant, participatively set goals clearly outperformed assigned ones, especially when a rationale was given.
questions.x: Participation tended to produce higher goals, and that is where its advantage came from. Once difficulty was equal, the source of the goal mattered little, so explaining the reason behind an assigned goal can work just as well.

questions.topic: Goal-Setting Theory: Specific, Difficult Goals and Performance
questions.t: On complex tasks where people lack the needed knowledge, a specific learning goal outperforms both a specific high performance goal and a do-your-best goal.
questions.f: On complex tasks where people lack the needed knowledge, a specific high performance goal outperforms both a specific learning goal and a do-your-best goal.
questions.x: A performance goal pushes people to execute before they know how, which can backfire. A learning goal, such as finding a set number of strategies, directs effort to building the knowledge first, as a 2004 business-simulation study showed.

questions.topic: Porter's Five Forces: Competitive Forces That Shape Industry Profitability
questions.t: Michael Porter first set out the five forces in a 1979 Harvard Business Review article, How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy, before developing them in Competitive Strategy (1980).
questions.f: Michael Porter first set out the five forces in his 1980 book Competitive Strategy, before summarizing them in a 1985 Harvard Business Review article, How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy.
questions.x: The HBR article came first, in 1979; the 1980 book paired the forces with the generic strategies of cost leadership, differentiation and focus. Porter revisited the framework in HBR in 2008.

questions.topic: Porter's Five Forces: Competitive Forces That Shape Industry Profitability
questions.t: In his 2008 restatement, Porter held that government policy and complementary products matter through their effect on the five forces rather than as forces of their own.
questions.f: In his 2008 restatement, Porter added government policy and complementary products as a sixth force acting alongside the original five.
questions.x: Porter resisted adding a sixth force: regulation or complements matter because they raise or lower entry barriers, buyer power and the rest. He also warned that fast growth does not guarantee profitability.

questions.topic: Porter's Five Forces: Competitive Forces That Shape Industry Profitability
questions.t: McGahan and Porter's 1997 study attributed about 19% of variance in US firms' profitability to industry and about 32% to business-specific effects.
questions.f: McGahan and Porter's 1997 study attributed about 32% of variance in US firms' profitability to industry and about 19% to business-specific effects.
questions.x: They were answering Rumelt's 1991 finding that industry effects were small. Their result showed industry matters, more in services than in manufacturing, but firm-level differences matter more, which resource-based critics stress.

questions.topic: Structured Problem Solving: The Consultant's Stepwise Method
questions.t: In Conn and McLean's seven-step cycle, teams prioritize by pruning the issue tree to branches that most affect the outcome and that they can actually influence.
questions.f: In Conn and McLean's seven-step cycle, teams prioritize by pruning the issue tree to branches that are easiest to measure, whether or not they can influence them.
questions.x: Prioritizing comes right after disaggregation and before planning the work. It keeps scarce analysis effort on drivers that both matter and are actionable, rather than on what is merely convenient to analyze.

questions.topic: Structured Problem Solving: The Consultant's Stepwise Method
questions.t: Conn recommends keeping a one-day answer, the team's best current view of the solution, and warns that a long, fixed workplan signals the team has stopped iterating.
questions.f: Conn recommends holding back any answer until the analysis is complete, and warns that a short, flexible workplan signals the team has stopped iterating.
questions.x: The cycle is iterative: each pass refines a working answer rather than building toward a reveal. Conn also suggests letting the most junior members speak first to limit bias.

questions.topic: Structured Problem Solving: The Consultant's Stepwise Method
questions.t: Baer, Dirks and Nickerson argue that diverse teams facing complex, ill-structured problems tend to formulate them too narrowly, which narrows the search for solutions.
questions.f: Baer, Dirks and Nickerson argue that diverse teams facing complex, ill-structured problems tend to formulate them too broadly, which scatters the search for solutions.
questions.x: Their research supports the method's emphasis on the problem-definition step. They propose collaborative structured inquiry to broaden formulation, and the theory implies a fixed sequence will not help if step one is rushed.

questions.topic: Management Theory: From Classical Administration to Systems and Contingency Thinking
questions.t: Max Weber's ideal type of bureaucracy rests on legal authority, with authority vested in the office rather than in the person who holds it.
questions.f: Max Weber's ideal type of bureaucracy rests on charismatic authority, with authority vested in the person rather than in the office they hold.
questions.x: Weber's bureaucracy combines specialized roles, merit-based hiring, a clear hierarchy and written rules, so authority survives a change of officeholder. Merton later warned that such rules can become ends in themselves.

questions.topic: Management Theory: From Classical Administration to Systems and Contingency Thinking
questions.t: Contingency theory, associated with Joan Woodward, rejects universal rules: the right structure depends on the situation, such as a firm's production technology.
questions.f: Contingency theory, associated with Joan Woodward, seeks universal rules: the right structure is the same whatever a firm's production technology.
questions.x: Classical theorists looked for one best way to organize. Woodward's view is that the best design varies with circumstances, which is why managers today ask how technology, environment or strategy change the answer.

questions.topic: Management Theory: From Classical Administration to Systems and Contingency Thinking
questions.t: In 1961 Harold Koontz described a management theory jungle of six competing schools and blamed loose terminology and theorists' unwillingness to understand one another.
questions.f: In 1961 Harold Koontz described a management theory jungle of six competing schools and blamed too little theorizing and an excess of empirical testing.
questions.x: Koontz called for clearer definitions and for testing fundamental principles, not less testing. His critique shows the field's own scholars were among its sharpest critics.

questions.topic: Activity-Based Costing: Assigning Overhead by Activities
questions.t: Robin Cooper and Robert Kaplan crystallised the case for activity-based costing in a 1988 HBR article, Measure Costs Right: Make the Right Decisions.
questions.f: Robin Cooper and Robert Kaplan crystallised the case for activity-based costing in a 1998 HBR article, Measure Costs Right: Make the Right Decisions.
questions.x: By the late 1980s automation had shrunk labour and swollen overhead, so labour-hour allocation distorted product costs. Cooper and Kaplan argued ABC could run alongside the official cost system rather than replace it.

questions.topic: Activity-Based Costing: Assigning Overhead by Activities
questions.t: Switching to activity-based costing usually raises the unit cost of low-volume products, because batch- and product-level costs like setups are spread over few units.
questions.f: Switching to activity-based costing usually lowers the unit cost of low-volume products, because batch- and product-level costs like setups are spread over many units.
questions.x: A single labour-hour rate lets high-volume products subsidize low-volume ones. ABC assigns setup and engineering costs to the products that cause them, revealing losses the old system hid.

questions.topic: Activity-Based Costing: Assigning Overhead by Activities
questions.t: Kaplan and Anderson argued conventional ABC's employee time surveys implicitly assumed staff were fully utilised, hiding idle capacity that time-driven ABC exposes.
questions.f: Kaplan and Anderson argued conventional ABC's employee time surveys implicitly assumed staff were half idle, overstating unused capacity that time-driven ABC corrects.
questions.x: When people report how they split their time, the shares add up to 100%, so slack disappears. Time-driven ABC uses capacity cost per minute and activity times, so unused capacity shows up explicitly.

questions.topic: Board of Directors: The Corporation's Elected Monitors
questions.t: Under Delaware's default rules, directors on a classified board can be removed by shareholders only for cause, while other directors can be removed with or without cause.
questions.f: Under Delaware's default rules, directors on a classified board can be removed by shareholders with or without cause, while other directors can be removed only for cause.
questions.x: A staggered board puts only part of its seats up for election each year, and the for-cause default adds further protection. Together they make it harder for shareholders to replace a board quickly.

questions.topic: Scientific Management: Taylor's System of Task Study and Standardized Work
questions.t: Frederick Taylor began timing shop tasks with a stopwatch at Midvale Steel in 1881, work that became the base of scientific management.
questions.f: Frederick Taylor began timing shop tasks with a stopwatch at Bethlehem Steel in 1881, work that became the base of scientific management.
questions.x: Taylor joined Midvale as a laborer in 1878 and started his time studies there. Bethlehem Steel came later, as his biggest consulting client, where he ran the shoveling and pig-iron studies.

questions.topic: Scientific Management: Taylor's System of Task Study and Standardized Work
questions.t: Taylor saw soldiering, the deliberate holding down of output, mainly as workers' systematic defence against piece-rate cuts and job losses.
questions.f: Taylor saw soldiering, the deliberate holding down of output, mainly as workers' natural laziness rather than a defence against piece-rate cuts.
questions.x: Taylor granted some natural inclination to take it easy, but blamed most restriction of output on workers protecting themselves from rate cuts and layoffs. That is why he argued higher productivity had to benefit both employer and employee.

questions.topic: Scientific Management: Taylor's System of Task Study and Standardized Work
questions.t: Historian Charles Wrege argued that Taylor's assistants largely ran the pig-iron studies and that Morris L. Cooke substantially drafted Taylor's 1911 book.
questions.f: Historian Charles Wrege argued that Taylor's assistants largely ran the pig-iron studies and that Henry Gantt substantially drafted Taylor's 1911 book.
questions.x: After decades in the Taylor archives, Wrege concluded the famous anecdotes in The Principles of Scientific Management were embellished and the text owed much to Cooke. Gantt was a Taylor associate known for his progress chart, not for writing the book.

questions.topic: Subscription Business Model: Selling Ongoing Access
questions.t: In the shifted-beta-geometric model, a subscriber cohort's retention rate rises over time because high-churn customers leave first, not because individuals grow more loyal.
questions.f: In the shifted-beta-geometric model, a subscriber cohort's retention rate rises over time because individuals grow more loyal, not because high-churn customers leave first.
questions.x: Fader and Hardie give each customer a constant churn probability that varies across customers. As the churn-prone drop out, the survivors are the low-churn types, so aggregate retention climbs even though nobody's own probability changes.

questions.topic: Subscription Business Model: Selling Ongoing Access
questions.t: Lambrecht and Skiera found that internet customers who picked a flat rate when pay-per-use was cheaper did not churn significantly more, while those wrongly on pay-per-use churned much more.
questions.f: Lambrecht and Skiera found that internet customers who picked a flat rate when pay-per-use was cheaper churned much more, while those wrongly on pay-per-use did not churn significantly more.
questions.x: Customers paid extra for a flat rate to insure against variable bills, enjoy usage without a running meter, or because they overestimated use. That bias raised profit without raising churn, which is part of why flat-rate subscriptions can beat their unit economics.

questions.topic: Subscription Business Model: Selling Ongoing Access
questions.t: Research summarized in 2023 reported that subscription-based firms had grown 3.7 times faster than the S&P 500 over the preceding decade.
questions.f: Research summarized in 2023 reported that subscription-based firms had grown 1.7 times faster than the S&P 500 over the preceding decade.
questions.x: Ofek and Konary cited this growth gap alongside the finding that nearly three-quarters of direct-to-consumer companies offered a subscription option, showing how mainstream the model had become.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model: Pricing Systematic Risk
questions.t: William Sharpe published the capital asset pricing model in The Journal of Finance in 1964, building on portfolio theory Harry Markowitz introduced in 1952.
questions.f: William Sharpe published the capital asset pricing model in The Journal of Finance in 1964, building on portfolio theory Merton Miller introduced in 1952.
questions.x: Markowitz's 1952 portfolio theory showed how diversification reduces risk; Sharpe asked what that implies for prices in equilibrium. Miller shared the 1990 Nobel with both men, but for corporate finance work, not portfolio theory.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model: Pricing Systematic Risk
questions.t: In the CAPM, only systematic risk earns a reward, because company-specific risk cancels out in a diversified portfolio.
questions.f: In the CAPM, only company-specific risk earns a reward, because systematic risk cancels out in a diversified portfolio.
questions.x: Diversification can wash out risks peculiar to one firm but not market-wide swings, so investors are paid only for bearing the latter. Beta measures that market exposure, which is why it is the model's single risk input.

questions.topic: Capital Asset Pricing Model: Pricing Systematic Risk
questions.t: Tests of the CAPM found the return-beta line too flat: low-beta stocks earned more, and high-beta stocks less, than the model predicts.
questions.f: Tests of the CAPM found the return-beta line too steep: low-beta stocks earned less, and high-beta stocks more, than the model predicts.
questions.x: In Fama and French's beta-sorted portfolios for 1928–2003, the lowest-beta group beat its prediction while the highest-beta group fell short. Returns rose with beta, just much less steeply than theory says.

questions.topic: Small Business Set-Asides: Reserving Federal Contracts for Small Firms
questions.t: Under the federal rule of two, work must be set aside when a contracting officer expects offers from two or more responsible small businesses at fair market prices.
questions.f: Under the federal rule of two, work must be set aside when a contracting officer expects offers from three or more responsible small businesses at fair market prices.
questions.x: The rule's name is its threshold: two credible small-business offers are enough to expect real price competition among small firms. Market research and past buying history inform the judgment, but the test itself is the reasonable expectation of two such offers.

questions.topic: Small Business Set-Asides: Reserving Federal Contracts for Small Firms
questions.t: Nakabayashi estimated that removing set-asides in Japanese public construction would drive out about 40% of small firms and raise procurement costs overall.
questions.f: Nakabayashi estimated that removing set-asides in Japanese public construction would drive out about 40% of small firms but lower procurement costs overall.
questions.x: In that market the protected firms would exit without set-asides, and the lost competition costs more than the efficiency gained. US timber-sale evidence points the other way, so a set-aside's cost depends on whether small firms would otherwise stay in.

questions.topic: Small Business Set-Asides: Reserving Federal Contracts for Small Firms
questions.t: In Kingdomware (2016), a unanimous Supreme Court held that the VA's veteran-business rule of two applies to every covered contract, even after its annual goals are met.
questions.f: In Kingdomware (2016), a unanimous Supreme Court held that the VA's veteran-business rule of two becomes optional for contracts once its annual goals are met.
questions.x: The VA had treated the rule as a target it could stop applying after hitting its goals. Justice Thomas's opinion read the statute's 'shall' as a duty covering each contract, including Federal Supply Schedule orders.

questions.topic: Open Innovation: Purposive Inflows and Outflows of Knowledge
questions.t: In open innovation's inside-out mode, unused internal ideas leave the firm through out-licensing, spin-outs and corporate venture capital.
questions.f: In open innovation's outside-in mode, unused internal ideas leave the firm through out-licensing, spin-outs and corporate venture capital.
questions.x: Chesbrough and Bogers separate inbound flows (outside-in: scouting, in-licensing, crowdsourcing) from outbound ones (inside-out: letting ideas that don't fit the business model reach market elsewhere). A coupled mode combines both with partners.

questions.topic: Open Innovation: Purposive Inflows and Outflows of Knowledge
questions.t: Chesbrough's false negatives are projects a closed firm judged unpromising that later proved valuable elsewhere, as with technologies from Xerox PARC.
questions.f: Chesbrough's false positives are projects a closed firm judged unpromising that later proved valuable elsewhere, as with technologies from Xerox PARC.
questions.x: A false negative is a wrong 'no': the firm rejects something that is actually worth a lot. Chesbrough used these lost opportunities to argue that closed innovation wastes value a firm could capture by licensing or spinning ideas out.

questions.topic: Open Innovation: Purposive Inflows and Outflows of Knowledge
questions.t: Laursen and Salter's 2006 study of UK manufacturers found that drawing on more external knowledge sources helps innovation only up to a point, forming an inverted U.
questions.f: Laursen and Salter's 2006 study of UK manufacturers found that drawing on more external knowledge sources hurts innovation only up to a point, forming a U shape.
questions.x: Broader and deeper external search both raised innovation at first and then turned negative, implying firms can over-search and spread attention too thin. The study of 2,707 firms is the best-known empirical test of open innovation.

questions.topic: Transaction Cost Economics: Markets, Hierarchies and the Make-or-Buy Decision
questions.t: Ronald Coase's 1937 article The Nature of the Firm argued that firms exist because using the market carries costs of negotiating and monitoring contracts.
questions.f: Ronald Coase's 1937 article The Nature of the Firm argued that firms exist because managerial authority carries costs of negotiating and monitoring contracts.
questions.x: Coase asked why so much allocation happens by command inside firms if prices allocate resources. His answer: markets are not free to use, so a firm grows until one more internal transaction would cost more than buying it outside.

questions.topic: Transaction Cost Economics: Markets, Hierarchies and the Make-or-Buy Decision
questions.t: In transaction cost economics, high asset specificity turns competitive bidding into small-numbers bargaining, which makes hierarchy more attractive than market buying.
questions.f: In transaction cost economics, high asset specificity turns small-numbers bargaining into competitive bidding, which makes market buying more attractive than hierarchy.
questions.x: Once investments are tailored to one relationship, they lose value elsewhere, so each side can hold the other up. Williamson predicted generic inputs get bought while specific ones are better made in-house or protected by contract.

questions.topic: Transaction Cost Economics: Markets, Hierarchies and the Make-or-Buy Decision
questions.t: Monteverde and Teece found that U.S. auto components needing specialized engineering know-how were more likely to be made in-house.
questions.f: Monteverde and Teece found that U.S. auto components needing specialized engineering know-how were more likely to be bought from outside suppliers.
questions.x: Their probit study was an early test of TCE: know-how tied to a particular car maker is a specific asset, so integration protects it from hold-up. The result matched Williamson's prediction.

questions.topic: Pricing Strategy: Value-Based, Cost-Based and Competition-Based Pricing
questions.t: Averaging pricing studies from 1983–2006, Hinterhuber found only about 17% of firms set prices from customer value, versus about 44% from competition.
questions.f: Averaging pricing studies from 1983–2006, Hinterhuber found about 44% of firms set prices from customer value, versus only about 17% from competition.
questions.x: Competition-based pricing was most common and cost-based came second at about 37%, leaving value-based pricing last even though scholars rate it the strongest approach. Hinterhuber traced the gap to obstacles such as hard-to-assess value and discount-prone sales forces.

questions.topic: Pricing Strategy: Value-Based, Cost-Based and Competition-Based Pricing
questions.t: A study of digital camera launches found plain market pricing was far more common than either price skimming or penetration pricing.
questions.f: A study of digital camera launches found price skimming was far more common than either plain market pricing or penetration pricing.
questions.x: Spann, Fischer and Tellis found skimming and penetration each described only about a fifth of launch paths, with market pricing covering the rest. Crowded markets and late entry left little room for a distinct strategic price.

questions.topic: Pricing Strategy: Value-Based, Cost-Based and Competition-Based Pricing
questions.t: In pricing practice, unit cost sets the floor, competitors' prices set a reference point, and customer value sets the ceiling a strategy tries to approach.
questions.f: In pricing practice, customer value sets the floor, competitors' prices set a reference point, and unit cost sets the ceiling a strategy tries to approach.
questions.x: Pricing below cost loses money on each unit, while buyers will not pay more than the product is worth to them. A supermarket that priced a yogurt from cost alone risked leaving money on the table below that value ceiling.

questions.topic: Toyota Production System (TPS): Waste Elimination Through Just-in-Time Flow and Built-in Quality
questions.t: Toyota credits just-in-time to Kiichiro Toyoda's flow production, and traces jidoka to Sakichi Toyoda's looms that stopped when a thread broke.
questions.f: Toyota credits just-in-time to Sakichi Toyoda's flow production, and traces jidoka to Kiichiro Toyoda's looms that stopped when a thread broke.
questions.x: The two pillars come from two generations: Sakichi's self-stopping looms (from 1896) gave jidoka, and Kiichiro installed conveyor flow production in 1927. Taiichi Ohno later combined them into a working system after the war.

questions.topic: Toyota Production System (TPS): Waste Elimination Through Just-in-Time Flow and Built-in Quality
questions.t: Spear and Bowen argued that TPS's tightly specified work makes it flexible, because each specification acts as a hypothesis that exposes problems.
questions.f: Spear and Bowen argued that TPS's loosely specified work makes it flexible, because workers are free to improvise around problems as they arise.
questions.x: After studying over 40 plants, they said the system's real engine is four unwritten rules. Scripting work precisely means any deviation is visible at once, so it can be fixed and the standard improved.

questions.topic: Toyota Production System (TPS): Waste Elimination Through Just-in-Time Flow and Built-in Quality
questions.t: In 1983 Toyota turned its inventory about 36 times, versus roughly 11 to 12 times for the U.S. automakers.
questions.f: In 1983 Toyota turned its inventory about 12 times, versus roughly 36 times for the U.S. automakers.
questions.x: Cusumano's comparison shows how little stock just-in-time leaves in the system. Because Toyota was also more capital-intensive per car, the gap was credited to the system as a whole rather than to cheap labor.

questions.topic: Organizational Learning: How Organizations Acquire, Retain and Transfer Knowledge
questions.t: Argyris's double-loop learning both corrects an action after an error and questions the assumptions and goals that lay behind the action.
questions.f: Argyris's single-loop learning both corrects an action after an error and questions the assumptions and goals that lay behind the action.
questions.x: Single-loop learning only fixes the action, like a thermostat switching on heat below 68 degrees. Double-loop learning also asks why the setting is 68, which is harder because it challenges the learner's own reasoning.

questions.topic: Organizational Learning: How Organizations Acquire, Retain and Transfer Knowledge
questions.t: In a competency trap, good results with an inferior routine build so much experience with it that a superior alternative is never adopted.
questions.f: In superstitious learning, good results with an inferior routine build so much experience with it that a superior alternative is never adopted.
questions.x: Levitt and March named both pathologies. The competency trap is about experience locking in a second-best routine; superstitious learning is drawing confident but wrong conclusions about what caused an outcome.

questions.topic: Organizational Learning: How Organizations Acquire, Retain and Transfer Knowledge
questions.t: In Huber's 1991 review, grafting means acquiring knowledge by bringing in members or units that already hold it, unlike vicarious learning from watching other firms.
questions.f: In Huber's 1991 review, vicarious learning means acquiring knowledge by bringing in members or units that already hold it, unlike grafting from watching other firms.
questions.x: Huber listed five routes to knowledge: what the firm knew at founding, its own experience, observing others (vicarious), grafting on people or units, and searching the environment. Grafting imports knowledge with its carriers; vicarious learning copies by observation.

questions.topic: Scenario Planning: Strategy for Multiple Plausible Futures
questions.t: Pierre Wack set out Shell's scenario method in a 1985 Harvard Business Review article, after Shell's early-1970s scenarios had explored producers restricting oil supply.
questions.f: Pierre Wack set out Shell's scenario method in a 1965 Harvard Business Review article, after Shell's early-1960s scenarios had explored producers restricting oil supply.
questions.x: Shell began long-term studies in 1965 and ran its first formal scenario round in 1971. When the 1973 oil crisis hit, its managers had already considered a similar world; Wack wrote up the method more than a decade later.

questions.topic: Scenario Planning: Strategy for Multiple Plausible Futures
questions.t: Wack distinguished predetermined elements, developments already in motion whose consequences can be traced, from critical uncertainties that remain genuinely open.
questions.f: Wack distinguished critical uncertainties, developments already in motion whose consequences can be traced, from predetermined elements that remain genuinely open.
questions.x: Demographic or supply trends already under way can be projected; truly open questions cannot. Treating an uncertainty as settled, or hiding it, is what makes plans brittle, so scenarios vary the uncertainties while holding the predetermined elements.

questions.topic: Scenario Planning: Strategy for Multiple Plausible Futures
questions.t: Field experiments by Phadnis and colleagues found that using multiple scenarios did not systematically change experts' overall confidence, but did push them toward more flexible investments.
questions.f: Field experiments by Phadnis and colleagues found that using multiple scenarios systematically lowered experts' overall confidence, but did not push them toward more flexible investments.
questions.x: Their 2014 study with infrastructure experts is one of the few rigorous tests. Judgments shifted toward the scenario considered and flexible options gained favor, yet with no control group it shows effects on judgment, not on outcomes.

questions.topic: Separation of Ownership and Control: Dispersed Shareholders and Managerial Power
questions.t: Fama and Jensen argued open corporations contain agency problems by separating decision management, initiating choices, from decision control, ratifying and monitoring them.
questions.f: Fama and Jensen argued open corporations contain agency problems by separating decision control, initiating choices, from decision management, ratifying and monitoring them.
questions.x: Managers propose and implement, while boards, internal hierarchies and ultimately the takeover market approve and check. Splitting these roles lets dispersed shareholders bear risk without trusting managers to police themselves.

questions.topic: Separation of Ownership and Control: Dispersed Shareholders and Managerial Power
questions.t: La Porta and colleagues found widely held large firms are rare outside countries with very good shareholder protection; elsewhere most are controlled by families or the state.
questions.f: La Porta and colleagues found widely held large firms are rare outside countries with weak shareholder protection; elsewhere most are controlled by families or the state.
questions.x: Their 1999 study of 27 wealthy economies showed the Berle-Means dispersed firm is mostly an American and British pattern. Where investors are poorly protected, controlling owners, often via pyramids, keep control instead.

questions.topic: Separation of Ownership and Control: Dispersed Shareholders and Managerial Power
questions.t: As of April 1, 2026, Mark Zuckerberg held about 60.8% of Meta's total voting power, largely through its ten-vote Class B shares.
questions.f: As of April 1, 2026, Mark Zuckerberg held about 99.8% of Meta's total voting power, largely through its ten-vote Class B shares.
questions.x: He owned 99.8% of the Class B shares, which translated into about 60.8% of all votes. That majority makes Meta a controlled company, the reverse of the manager-dominated firm Berle and Means described.

questions.topic: Delphi Method: Iterative Anonymous Expert Consensus
questions.t: The Delphi method was developed at the RAND Corporation in the 1950s, and Norman Dalkey and Olaf Helmer described an experiment with it in 1963.
questions.f: The Delphi method was developed at the RAND Corporation in the 1970s, and Norman Dalkey and Olaf Helmer described an experiment with it in 1983.
questions.x: Their 1963 Management Science article framed the aim as reaching the most reliable consensus of experts through questionnaires with controlled feedback. RAND's 1964 long-range forecasting study then showed the method at scale.

questions.topic: Delphi Method: Iterative Anonymous Expert Consensus
questions.t: In a classical Delphi, panellists stay anonymous to one another and the group answer is computed statistically rather than negotiated in discussion.
questions.f: In a classical Delphi, panellists meet face to face and the group answer is negotiated in discussion rather than computed statistically.
questions.x: Anonymity and statistical aggregation, such as a median with quartiles, stop eloquent speakers or senior figures from swaying the panel. Experts see the group summary between rounds and may revise their own answers.

questions.topic: Delphi Method: Iterative Anonymous Expert Consensus
questions.t: Rowe and Wright's 1999 review found Delphi groups usually beat unstructured interacting groups but showed no consistent edge over other structured group methods.
questions.f: Rowe and Wright's 1999 review found Delphi groups usually beat other structured group methods but showed no consistent edge over unstructured interacting groups.
questions.x: Delphi mostly outperformed simple averages and free discussion, yet techniques like the nominal group method did about as well. They also warned that lab versions often strayed from the original design.

questions.topic: Performance Management: Planning, Appraising and Developing Employee Performance
questions.t: Performance appraisal, the periodic rating of an individual, is one step within performance management, which also covers what managers do before and after the rating.
questions.f: Performance management, the periodic rating of an individual, is one step within performance appraisal, which also covers what managers do before and after the rating.
questions.x: OPM's cycle runs from planning and monitoring through developing, rating and rewarding. Appraisal is just the rating stage, so a firm can drop or redesign ratings while still managing performance.

questions.topic: Performance Management: Planning, Appraising and Developing Employee Performance
questions.t: Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis found feedback had a positive average effect on performance, yet over one-third of feedback interventions reduced it.
questions.f: Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis found feedback had a negative average effect on performance, though over one-third of feedback interventions improved it.
questions.x: Across 607 effect sizes the average gain was moderate, but the spread was wide enough that feedback often backfired. That is why feedback, the core of most systems, cannot be assumed to help.

questions.topic: Performance Management: Planning, Appraising and Developing Employee Performance
questions.t: In Deloitte's 2015 redesign, team leaders answered questions about future actions they would take for each person instead of rating that person's skills.
questions.f: In Deloitte's 2015 redesign, team leaders rated each person's skills on a detailed scale instead of answering questions about future actions they would take.
questions.x: Research on idiosyncratic rater effects showed skill ratings say more about the rater than the person rated. Asking about the leader's own intended actions, such as promotion, aimed to give more reliable, forward-looking data.

questions.topic: DuPont Analysis: Decomposing Return on Equity
questions.t: In the three-step DuPont formula, ROE equals profit margin times total asset turnover times the equity multiplier, total assets over shareholders' equity.
questions.f: In the three-step DuPont formula, ROE equals profit margin times total asset turnover times the debt ratio, total liabilities over total assets.
questions.x: Sales and total assets cancel across the three ratios, leaving net income over equity. The equity multiplier is the leverage term: the more assets financed by liabilities, the higher it is.

questions.topic: DuPont Analysis: Decomposing Return on Equity
questions.t: Donaldson Brown devised DuPont's return-on-investment measure in 1914 and, after moving to General Motors in 1921, adapted it into a target-return pricing method.
questions.f: Donaldson Brown devised General Motors' return-on-investment measure in 1914 and, after moving to DuPont in 1921, adapted it into a target-return pricing method.
questions.x: Brown combined earnings, working capital and plant investment into one ROI figure at DuPont. At GM each division set a target return and standard volume, then worked out the price needed to hit it.

questions.topic: DuPont Analysis: Decomposing Return on Equity
questions.t: Nissim and Penman argued the standard DuPont identity mixes operating and financing activities, so they split ROE into operating return plus a leverage-times-spread term.
questions.f: Nissim and Penman argued the standard DuPont identity overstates operating returns, so they replaced ROE with return on total assets plus a leverage-times-spread term.
questions.x: Their 2001 analysis treats operations as the source of value and separates out how borrowing adds or subtracts from it. They found return on total assets actually understates operating profitability because it blends in financial items.

questions.topic: Enron Scandal: Off-Balance-Sheet Fraud and the 2001 Collapse of Enron
questions.t: The SEC alleged that Enron's CFO used special purpose entities he secretly controlled so that Enron overstated net income and understated debt.
questions.f: The SEC alleged that Enron's CFO used special purpose entities he secretly controlled so that Enron understated net income and overstated debt.
questions.x: A properly independent SPE can keep assets and debt off the sponsor's balance sheet. Because Fastow controlled vehicles like Chewco and LJM, or they were guaranteed against loss, they were not truly independent, so the deals flattered profits and hid borrowing.

questions.topic: Enron Scandal: Off-Balance-Sheet Fraud and the 2001 Collapse of Enron
questions.t: A 2002 Senate subcommittee found Enron's board had waived its code of conduct so CFO Andrew Fastow could run the LJM partnerships.
questions.f: A 2002 Senate subcommittee found Enron's board had waived its code of conduct so CEO Jeffrey Skilling could run the LJM partnerships.
questions.x: Letting the finance chief run funds that traded with Enron was a glaring conflict of interest. The subcommittee cited it among the board's failures of fiduciary duty and rejected directors' claims that they had simply relied on advisers.

questions.topic: Enron Scandal: Off-Balance-Sheet Fraud and the 2001 Collapse of Enron
questions.t: By an October 2000 Enron presentation, about $27 billion of its roughly $60 billion in assets sat with unconsolidated affiliates.
questions.f: By an October 2000 Enron presentation, about $7 billion of its roughly $60 billion in assets sat with unconsolidated affiliates.
questions.x: Nearly half of Enron's assets were held outside its consolidated statements, and its annual reports listed almost 3,000 related entities. That scale is why off-balance-sheet vehicles were central to the fraud.

questions.topic: Long Tail: Aggregating Demand for Niche Products
questions.t: Chris Anderson, then editor of Wired, introduced the long tail in the magazine's October 2004 issue and later expanded it into a book.
questions.f: Chris Anderson, then editor of Wired, introduced the long tail in the magazine's October 2008 issue and later expanded it into a book.
questions.x: Anderson built the idea on 2004 data from Amazon, Netflix and Rhapsody showing large sales outside the titles a physical store could stock. 2008 is the year of Anita Elberse's best-known critique in Harvard Business Review.

questions.topic: Long Tail: Aggregating Demand for Niche Products
questions.t: A retailer selling the same products at the same prices online and by catalog had less concentrated online sales, pointing to lower search costs as a cause of the long tail.
questions.f: A retailer selling the same products at the same prices online and by catalog had equally concentrated sales in both, pointing to wider selection alone as the cause of the long tail.
questions.x: Brynjolfsson, Hu and Simester held selection and price fixed, yet online buyers still bought more niche items, especially those using search and recommendations. So discovery tools, not only bigger catalogs, push demand into the tail.

questions.topic: Long Tail: Aggregating Demand for Niche Products
questions.t: Greater variety at online booksellers raised U.S. consumer welfare by an estimated $731 million to $1.03 billion in 2000, 7 to 10 times the gain from lower prices.
questions.f: Greater variety at online booksellers raised U.S. consumer welfare by an estimated $731 million to $1.03 billion in 2000, about one-tenth the gain from lower prices.
questions.x: Brynjolfsson, Hu and Smith found Amazon offered over 23 times the titles of a typical superstore. Access to obscure books, not cheaper prices, was the main benefit of online bookselling to consumers.

questions.topic: Capital Structure: The Mix of Debt and Equity Financing
questions.t: Under the pecking order theory, firms use internal funds first, then debt, and issue equity last, since investors read a stock issue as a sign of overvalued shares.
questions.f: Under the pecking order theory, firms use internal funds first, then equity, and issue debt last, since investors read a bond issue as a sign of overvalued shares.
questions.x: Myers tied the ordering to asymmetric information: managers know more than outsiders, so selling stock signals they think it is overpriced. A firm's debt ratio then reflects its past need for outside money, not a target.

questions.topic: Capital Structure: The Mix of Debt and Equity Financing
questions.t: Baker and Wurgler found firms tend to issue equity when market-to-book ratios are high and repurchase when they are low, leaving a persistent mark on leverage.
questions.f: Baker and Wurgler found firms tend to issue equity when market-to-book ratios are low and repurchase when they are high, leaving a persistent mark on leverage.
questions.x: Firms sell shares when they look richly valued. Because the effect lasted years instead of being reversed toward a target, Baker and Wurgler saw capital structure as the cumulative result of timing the equity market.

questions.topic: Capital Structure: The Mix of Debt and Equity Financing
questions.t: Graham and Harvey's CFO survey found financial flexibility and credit ratings were the main concerns when issuing debt, while EPS dilution weighed most when issuing equity.
questions.f: Graham and Harvey's CFO survey found EPS dilution was the main concern when issuing debt, while financial flexibility and credit ratings weighed most when issuing equity.
questions.x: Executives care about keeping spare borrowing capacity and protecting their rating when they borrow, and about diluting earnings per share when they sell stock. The survey also found little sign that CFOs consciously weigh many mechanisms in academic models.

questions.topic: DFARS: Defense Department Rules Layered on Top of the FAR
questions.t: Before the FAR took effect in 1984, DoD bought under the Defense Acquisition Regulation, which had been called the Armed Services Procurement Regulation until 1978.
questions.f: Before the FAR took effect in 1984, DoD bought under the Defense Acquisition Regulation, which had been called the Federal Procurement Regulations until 1978.
questions.x: The Federal Procurement Regulations were the civilian agencies' rules. When the single FAR replaced both systems, DoD's remaining unique rules moved into the DFARS, codified right after the FAR in Title 48.

questions.topic: DFARS: Defense Department Rules Layered on Top of the FAR
questions.t: In the DFARS, purely supplemental text uses section numbers of 70 and up, while military department supplements use numbers of 90 and up.
questions.f: In the DFARS, purely supplemental text uses section numbers of 90 and up, while military department supplements use numbers of 70 and up.
questions.x: Text that implements a FAR rule keeps the FAR's numbering, so DFARS 201.3 parallels FAR 1.3. Reserved number ranges let readers tell at a glance whether a section implements the FAR, adds a DoD-wide rule or comes from a component.

questions.topic: DFARS: Defense Department Rules Layered on Top of the FAR
questions.t: The Section 809 Panel reported in 2018 that, of 165 government clauses for commercial-item buys under the FAR and DFARS, 122 came from statute.
questions.f: The Section 809 Panel reported in 2018 that, of 165 government clauses for commercial-item buys under the FAR and DFARS, 122 came from agency policy.
questions.x: The clause count had nearly tripled from 57 in 1995, but only 23 came from agency policy. So much of the complexity contractors blame on DoD actually rests on laws Congress passed.

questions.topic: Lean Startup: Validated Learning Through the Build-Measure-Learn Loop
questions.t: Eric Ries created the lean startup by combining Steve Blank's customer development with agile software practices, naming it after lean manufacturing.
questions.f: Steve Blank created the lean startup by combining Eric Ries's customer development with agile software practices, naming it after lean manufacturing.
questions.x: Blank developed customer development and published it in 2003; Ries, a founder Blank advised, added agile methods and the lean label, then wrote The Lean Startup in 2011. The name nods to Toyota's war on waste.

questions.topic: Lean Startup: Validated Learning Through the Build-Measure-Learn Loop
questions.t: Steve Blank defines a startup as a temporary organization searching for a repeatable, scalable business model, not a small company executing a known one.
questions.f: Steve Blank defines a startup as a temporary organization executing a known, scalable business model, not a small company still searching for one.
questions.x: Because a startup does not yet know its customers, channels or revenue model, writing a detailed plan is premature. Blank's definition is why lean startup treats the business model as hypotheses to test.

questions.topic: Lean Startup: Validated Learning Through the Build-Measure-Learn Loop
questions.t: Felin, Gambardella, Stern and Zenger argue lean startup's reliance on quick customer feedback steers founders toward incremental rather than truly novel opportunities.
questions.f: Felin, Gambardella, Stern and Zenger argue lean startup's reliance on quick customer feedback steers founders toward truly novel rather than incremental opportunities.
questions.x: Customers find it hard to judge products unlike anything they know, so fast validation favours safe ideas. The authors suggest starting from a theory of value and running critical experiments, a stance known as the theory-based view.

questions.topic: Adverse Selection: Hidden Information Before a Contract
questions.t: Besides used cars, Akerlof's 1970 lemons paper analysed health insurance for people over 65, an argument he used in favour of a public scheme like Medicare.
questions.f: Besides used cars, Akerlof's 1970 lemons paper analysed health insurance for low-income families, an argument he used in favour of a public scheme like Medicaid.
questions.x: As premiums for older people rise, those who remain are increasingly the ones expecting to need care, so there may be no price at which policies sell. A public scheme sidesteps that unravelling.

questions.topic: Adverse Selection: Hidden Information Before a Contract
questions.t: In Rothschild and Stiglitz's separating equilibrium, high-risk buyers get full insurance at fair odds, while low-risk buyers get only partial cover.
questions.f: In Rothschild and Stiglitz's separating equilibrium, low-risk buyers get full insurance at fair odds, while high-risk buyers get only partial cover.
questions.x: Insurers cannot see risk, so they ration cover for the cheap policy to make it unattractive to high-risk buyers, who would otherwise mimic the low-risk type. The low-risk group bears the cost, and nobody gains from it.

questions.topic: Adverse Selection: Hidden Information Before a Contract
questions.t: Cutler and Reber found that Harvard's mid-1990s switch to equal health-plan contributions set off adverse selection, yet lower premiums meant welfare rose overall.
questions.f: Cutler and Reber found that Harvard's mid-1990s switch to equal health-plan contributions set off adverse selection, and its losses outweighed lower premiums so welfare fell overall.
questions.x: Selection cost about 2% of baseline health spending, but competition cut Harvard's premiums nearly 10% relative to the Boston area. It is the cleanest documented death spiral, and still a net gain.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix: The Four Ps of Product, Price, Place and Promotion
questions.t: Neil Borden popularised the term marketing mix, and E. Jerome McCarthy later condensed Borden's list of twelve ingredients into the four Ps.
questions.f: E. Jerome McCarthy popularised the term marketing mix, and Neil Borden later condensed McCarthy's list of twelve ingredients into the four Ps.
questions.x: Borden's twelve ingredients ran from product planning and pricing to packaging, display and fact finding. McCarthy's simpler product, price, place and promotion became the dominant teaching framework.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix: The Four Ps of Product, Price, Place and Promotion
questions.t: Constantinides' 2006 review found two weaknesses of the 4Ps common across marketing fields: an internal, seller-side orientation and no room for personalisation.
questions.f: Constantinides' 2006 review found two weaknesses of the 4Ps common across marketing fields: an external, customer-side orientation and too much room for personalisation.
questions.x: The mix was built for mass markets and describes what the seller controls, not what customers need. That gap is why relationship and services marketers proposed alternatives or extensions.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix: The Four Ps of Product, Price, Place and Promotion
questions.t: For services, Booms and Bitner extended the mix to 7Ps by adding people, physical evidence and process to product, price, place and promotion.
questions.f: For services, Booms and Bitner extended the mix to 7Ps by adding people, packaging and positioning to product, price, place and promotion.
questions.x: In a service the staff, the setting and the delivery process are part of what the customer buys, so the original four levers missed them. Their 1981 proposal became the standard services-marketing mix.

questions.topic: Lean Manufacturing: Eliminating Waste Across the Value Stream
questions.t: The Machine That Changed the World (1990) defined lean largely by outcomes, and Lean Thinking (1996) recast it as a roadmap any organization could follow.
questions.f: Lean Thinking (1990) defined lean largely by outcomes, and The Machine That Changed the World (1996) recast it as a roadmap any organization could follow.
questions.x: The MIT car-industry study showed lean plants doing more with less than mass producers. Womack and Jones's later book turned those findings into principles, and the Lean Enterprise Institute followed in 1997 to spread them.

questions.topic: Lean Manufacturing: Eliminating Waste Across the Value Stream
questions.t: In Womack and Jones's five lean principles, the customer pulls production wherever continuous flow is not yet possible.
questions.f: In Womack and Jones's five lean principles, a forecast pushes production wherever continuous flow is not yet possible.
questions.x: The principles run from specifying value and mapping the value stream to creating flow, then pull, then pursuing perfection. Pull means nothing is made until downstream demand asks for it, which keeps inventory from piling up.

questions.topic: Lean Manufacturing: Eliminating Waste Across the Value Stream
questions.t: A study of 351 pharmaceutical plants found hard lean practices like just-in-time improved performance directly, while soft practices acted only as moderators.
questions.f: A study of 351 pharmaceutical plants found soft lean practices like empowerment improved performance directly, while hard practices acted only as moderators.
questions.x: Just-in-time, TQM and total productive maintenance raised operational results on their own. Empowerment and visual management amplified those gains, whereas rigid standardization and heavy goal setting seemed to weaken them.

questions.topic: Group Decision Making: How Groups Combine Individual Judgments into Choices
questions.t: Stoner's 1961 work found individuals became riskier after group discussion, a result later research generalized into group polarization.
questions.f: Stoner's 1961 work found individuals became more cautious after group discussion, a result later research generalized into group polarization.
questions.x: The 'risky shift' turned out to be one case of a broader pattern: discussion pushes like-minded members further in whatever direction they already leaned. More than 200 studies document it.

questions.topic: Group Decision Making: How Groups Combine Individual Judgments into Choices
