questions.t: In fiscal 2025 (FY2025), GAO sustained 53 of its 380 bid protest merit decisions, a sustain rate of about 14%.
questions.f: In fiscal 2025 (FY2025), GAO sustained 198 of its 380 bid protest merit decisions, a sustain rate of about 52%.
questions.x: Only about one merit decision in seven went the protester's way, which is why protests are rarer winners than their reputation suggests. The 52% figure is GAO's broader effectiveness rate, which also counts voluntary corrective action by agencies.

questions.topic: Bid Protest: Challenging Federal Contract Awards at GAO
questions.t: Penn State finance researchers found that firms winning a bid protest face a 68% lower chance of getting contracts from the contested agency over the next four years.
questions.f: Penn State finance researchers found that firms winning a bid protest enjoy a 68% higher chance of getting contracts from the contested agency over the next four years.
questions.x: The finding points to a hidden cost of protesting: even a successful challenge can sour the relationship with the buying agency. It sits alongside critiques that protests push agencies to over-document and favour price-driven or existing contract vehicles.

questions.topic: Customer Development: Steve Blank's Search for a Repeatable Business Model
questions.t: Steve Blank began outlining customer development in a Berkeley course in 2003 and set it out in detail that year in The Four Steps to the Epiphany.
questions.f: Steve Blank began outlining customer development in a Stanford course in 2011 and set it out in detail that year in The Four Steps to the Epiphany.
questions.x: Blank developed the method in 2003 after about two decades in startups, when he concluded the usual product development sequence ignored the biggest risk: having no customers. 2011 is when NSF launched its Innovation Corps program built on his ideas, not when he wrote the book.

questions.topic: Customer Development: Steve Blank's Search for a Repeatable Business Model
questions.t: In customer development, a startup whose validation evidence is weak pivots by changing one or more hypotheses and loops back to customer discovery.
questions.f: In customer development, a startup whose validation evidence is weak pivots by changing one or more hypotheses and moves ahead to customer creation.
questions.x: Customer creation, the push from a few customers to many, only makes sense once a repeatable sales roadmap and workable financial model have been validated. Weak evidence sends the team back to discovery to test revised hypotheses about the problem and solution.

questions.topic: Customer Development: Steve Blank's Search for a Repeatable Business Model
questions.t: As of 2026, NSF's I-Corps national teams program runs about seven weeks and requires each team to complete at least 100 interviews with potential customers and stakeholders.
questions.f: As of 2026, NSF's I-Corps national teams program runs about seven weeks and requires each team to complete at least 20 interviews with potential customers and stakeholders.
questions.x: I-Corps is the largest institutional application of customer development, and its high interview quota forces academic founders out of the lab to test their business model hypotheses. Teams also commit at least 15 hours a week and end with a lessons-learned presentation.

questions.topic: Churn Rate: Measuring Customer Attrition and Retention
questions.t: Reichheld and Sasser argued in a 1990 Harvard Business Review article that retaining just 5% more customers could raise profits by nearly 100% in the service businesses they studied.
questions.f: Reichheld and Sasser argued in a 1990 Harvard Business Review article that retaining just 5% more customers could raise profits by nearly 10% in the service businesses they studied.
questions.x: Their point was that defections can matter more to profit than scale, market share or unit cost, so the defection rate works as a leading indicator. A gain of only about 10% would not have supported that bold claim.

questions.topic: Churn Rate: Measuring Customer Attrition and Retention
questions.t: In a field experiment with about 65,000 mobile subscribers, proactively nudging users toward better-fitting plans raised churn from 6% to 10%.
questions.f: In a field experiment with about 65,000 mobile subscribers, proactively nudging users toward better-fitting plans cut churn from 10% to 6%.
questions.x: Ascarza, Iyengar and Schleicher found the outreach backfired, with the worst effects among customers whose usage was volatile or falling. It is a warning that retention campaigns should target customers whose behaviour they will actually change, not simply those at highest risk.

questions.topic: Churn Rate: Measuring Customer Attrition and Retention
questions.t: T-Mobile US reported branded postpaid phone churn of 1.18% for 2017, far below its branded prepaid churn of 4.04% that year.
questions.f: T-Mobile US reported branded prepaid churn of 1.18% for 2017, far below its branded postpaid phone churn of 4.04% that year.
questions.x: Postpaid phone customers left at roughly a quarter of the prepaid rate in 2017. T-Mobile credited part of that year's postpaid improvement to moving higher-churn customers to a wholesale partner, so reported churn can also change through who is counted.

questions.topic: Change Management: From Lewin's Unfreezing to Kotter's Eight Steps
questions.t: John Kotter based his eight-step change advice, in a 1995 Harvard Business Review article, on watching more than 100 companies such as Ford and British Airways attempt transformation.
questions.f: John Kotter based his eight-step change advice, in a 1975 Harvard Business Review article, on watching more than 100 companies such as Ford and British Airways attempt transformation.
questions.x: Kotter's 1995 article framed its advice as eight errors to avoid, from insufficient urgency to failing to anchor change in culture. He found a few efforts very successful, a few outright failures, and most in between, tilted toward the lower end.

questions.topic: Change Management: From Lewin's Unfreezing to Kotter's Eight Steps
questions.t: Kotter judged a sense of urgency sufficient only when roughly 75% of a company's management is convinced that business as usual is unacceptable.
questions.f: Kotter judged a sense of urgency sufficient only when roughly 50% of a company's management is convinced that business as usual is unacceptable.
questions.x: Kotter set a high bar, about three quarters of management, for the first step of establishing urgency. He found that well over half of the companies he watched failed at this first phase.

questions.topic: Change Management: From Lewin's Unfreezing to Kotter's Eight Steps
questions.t: Mark Hughes reviewed five published sources for the claim that about 70% of change initiatives fail and found that none gives valid, reliable evidence for it.
questions.f: Mark Hughes reviewed five published sources for the claim that about 70% of change initiatives fail and found that all five give valid, reliable evidence for it.
questions.x: The 70% failure rate is widely repeated, but Hughes traced it to sources that lack sound empirical support. It is a useful caution against treating a popular statistic as established fact.

questions.topic: Competitive Advantage: Why Some Firms Persistently Outperform Rivals
questions.t: Rumelt's 1991 decomposition of business-unit returns found large, stable business-unit effects, small industry effects and negligible corporate-parent effects.
questions.f: Rumelt's 1991 decomposition of business-unit returns found large, stable corporate-parent effects, small industry effects and negligible business-unit effects.
questions.x: Using FTC Line of Business data, Rumelt showed most economic rents come from business-specific sources, not from industry membership or the corporate parent. That finding challenged a purely industry-structure view and lent weight to resource-based explanations of advantage.
